summary: An independent-researcher process note. It reads productivity trials, GitHub agent-PR studies, repository-instruction papers, issue-resolution benchmarks, and hardware-verification results as evidence that agent speed does not by itself improve engineering outcomes, then proposes Agentic Agile-V: a conversation-to-brief gate, a SCOPE-V task loop, and risk-tiered evidence bundles. The framework is not tested.

claims.claim: Controlled studies do not support the claim that autonomous code generation automatically improves outcomes
claims.evidence: §II-B cites a Google RCT (96 engineers, about 21% less time on one enterprise task), a METR RCT (about 19% slowdown on mature open-source work), and a 2026 meta-analysis with a moderate heterogeneous effect. These are other papers' numbers, accurately hedged in §II, and not reanalyzed here.

claims.claim: Repository instruction files have mixed effects, so more context is not automatically better
claims.evidence: §II-C cites one study associating AGENTS.md with lower runtime and tokens, another where extra context files reduced success and raised cost, and a factorial study with little adherence effect from size, position, or local contradiction. No new measurement.

claims.claim: Agentic Agile-V (conversation, then a reviewed brief, then SCOPE-V, then a risk-tiered evidence bundle) is the process that turns intent into verifiable output
claims.evidence: Sections V–IX and Tables I–II specify artifacts and gates. §X-D and §XII say the framework is untested and list the comparisons (brief versus chat, independent tests, overhead) as future work. The hardware feasibility claim is delegated to a prior Agile-V case study, not repeated here.

claims.claim: Issue-resolution and hardware benchmarks show repository execution and RTL generation remain unreliable
claims.evidence: §II-D and §II-E summarize published benchmarks, including a cited 0% pass@1 figure on a RealBench hardware task. No table recomputes those results.

patterns.note: §VII-A says early conversation should produce a better problem statement, not code. That split is prescribed. The paper does not compare a discovery-then-brief workflow with coding from the chat.
The operational rule is to implement from a reviewed brief (objective, non-goals, acceptance criteria, evidence). It is consistent with cited context-file results and not tested as a gate.
The R2/R3 evidence bundle asks for a trace from acceptance criteria to tests, plus the plan, commands, and reviewer decision. No link is checked for correctness in this paper.
Clarifying requirements is listed as a use of conversation. The agent is not evaluated on whether it asks, or on whether asking helps.
Table II scales human approval from optional (throwaway) to explicit sign-off (security, medical, firmware). The tiers are a proposal.
The bug workflow says to add a failing regression test before the patch when possible. No test-first run is reported.
§II-C reports other studies that disagree on whether AGENTS.md helps. This paper recommends keeping such files short and current, without a new comparison.
Tests, lint, and simulation are required evidence in the Prove step, argued from cited trials rather than a new verifier ablation.

methodology.sample: Bounded narrative synthesis. Inclusion is any source on agentic coding, issue resolution, repository execution, productivity, configuration files, permission gating, hardware generation or verification, or traceability. No count of included or excluded papers.
methodology.baselines: None for the proposed framework. Cited contrasts are enterprise RCT versus open-source RCT, and helpful versus harmful context files.
methodology.variance: Not applicable. Heterogeneity of the cited effects is discussed qualitatively.
methodology.languages: Discussion covers software, firmware, and hardware. No Java evaluation.

standards.artifacts: Templates are printed in the paper (feature, bug, and hardware briefs). No dataset or protocol beyond the citation list.

biases.detail: SCOPE-V and Agile-V rename a V-model plus agile iteration plus a task brief. The paper cites an earlier Agile-V case study as the lifecycle it generalizes.
The abstract's conclusion that agentic AI increases the value of requirements and traceability is a design stance. The only measured claims in the paper are citations.
The evidence base is whatever the author judged relevant. There is no search protocol, flow diagram, or exclusion log, despite the 'bounded evidence synthesis' label.
Productivity and benchmark figures are taken from secondary sources and not rechecked against those papers' tables in this document.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None directly. Vendor tools appear as cited objects.
coi.detail: No employer or product is attached to the proposal.

verdict_reason: The cited split between enterprise speedup and open-source slowdown, and between helpful and harmful repository instructions, is a fair reading of other studies and matches a spec-before-code gate. Agentic Agile-V itself is an untested checklist. Nothing in this paper shows that the SCOPE-V loop, the evidence bundle, or the risk tiers change outcomes.
applicability: The useful rule for this team is operational and still a hypothesis: discovery can stay in conversation, and an agent should implement only from a reviewed brief that names non-goals, the repos and contracts touched, acceptance checks, and the commands that will be rerun. Bug work should start from a reproduction and a failing test, not a patch. Keep repository instruction files short. Do not adopt the four risk tiers or the hardware bundle as policy until someone measures brief-versus-chat on a real Java change. The paper has no multi-repo Java result and no data on whether the extra gates slow new developers.
